newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary bourse says rally will continue in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Hungary bourse says rally will continue in 1997.

text.p: The Budapest Stock Exchange (BSE) was likely to extend the gains which made it one of the best-performing bourses in the world last year, top BSE officials told a news conference on Wednesday.
"I do not see a trend which could stop the rising," BSE Chairman Zsigmond Jarai said, adding that 1996 was the Budapest bourse's most succesful year since it restarted its operations in 1991.

Jarai said that according to his information prices rose the most rapidly on the BSE among all the bourses in the world in 1996. He also said 50 percent of all shares listed on the Budapest exchange were now being traded here, compared to two thirds traded on the foreign depository market in London in 1995.
The BUX index has almost tripled since the beginning of last year, closing 1996 at 4,134.31 points, up from 1,528.92 on January 1, 1996, and rising further to 4,463.47 points by Tuesday.

The BUX had hit more than 10 successive daily record highs by Tuesday, to the surprise of BSE traders who expected downwards corrections could come any time. However, they believe that 1997 will raise the index substantially further.
Jarai said macroeconomic and corporate figures justified such optimism.
"The Hungarian economy will grow relatively rapidly in 1997," he said. "The companies produce better and better results and they are increasing their profits and exports quickly,".

Hungary expects two to three percent gross domestic product growth in 1997 following last year's stagnation, and Jarai said bourse companies were likely to be among the main beneficiaries of that growth.

Potential difficulties in the state sector, the government budget and social security were not likely to affect the firms listed on the BSE as these were mainly fully or partly privatised companies, he said.

He added that the BSE hoped to boost its capitalisation further in 1997, which could strengthen the interest of foreign investors, who were likely to remain the major players on the BSE until domestic pension funds spread in the next few years.
Jarai said the BSE increased its total capitalisation to 2,447.7 billion forints in 1996 from 1,221.3 billion in 1995 and planned to boost that figure.
He added that the BSE was engaged in negotiation with the state privatisation agency APV about bourse-listing a number of of large state-owned companies slated for sale. @
Jarai said the BSE was talking with the telecommunications company Matav, controlled by Deutsche Telekom AG and Ameritech Corp about listing its shares.

He added that he hoped that the oil and gas company MOL would increase the number of its shares on the BSE and that energy companies, in which large stakes were sold to western investors in 1995, would also be listed on the BSE.
Jarai said it was a significant that almost 50 percent of trading in Hungarian shares took place on the BSE in 1996, compared with 1995 when the market share of London's SEAQ was 67 percent.
The BSE also boosted its turnover in futures deals to 200 billion forints in 1996 from some 10 billion in 1995.

BSE Managing Director Jozsef Rotyis said the bourse was likely to open its standardised options market in June the earliest, and trading in non-standardised options, suspended last year for irregularities in trading, may be restarted in February.
He added that the BSE was likely to shift to the continuous calculation of the BUX index at the end of this month from the current daily fixing.
Rotyis said that foreigners would be allowed to trade in BUX index futures from January 24.
